item.title: Atmospheric Chemistry-Climate Modeling with an AI Foundation Model
item.description: arXiv:2610.22555v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Atmospheric composition and chemistry-climate interactions are central to predicting future climate change. Yet simulating chemical and aerosol processes is typically the most expensive component of an atmospheric model and is often highly simplified or prescribed entirely. AI weather forecasting foundation models have shown skill rivalling process-based models and are increasingly fine-tuned for new atmospheric tasks. Here, we present the first foundation model to capture interactions between emissions, atmospheric composition, and radiation. We fine-tune the Aurora Earth system foundation model on simulations from the chemistry-climate model UKCA. Our model reproduces daily meteorology, composition, aerosol, and radiation fields of the coupled system with 23 of 27 predicted fields achieving $R^2$ above 0.85 in both the troposphere and stratosphere. It reproduces ozone, CO, and temperature with annual mean biases below 4% and the downwelling shortwave and longwave fluxes to within 6%. Our model remains stable in autoregressive simulation over 50 years while running ~$100\times$ faster than UKCA. By training on paired emissions scenarios, our model learns responses to perturbations by capturing tropospheric ozone's response to changes in NO and CO emissions and surface radiation's response to aerosol. We further show that incorporating MLS satellite ozone retrievals into training corrects biases in the underlying UKCA fields, reducing zonal mean ozone error against collocated observations by 23% between 250 and 20 hPa. Our approach does not suggest process-based modeling can be replaced but demonstrates that a foundation model can be adapted to respond to forcings and learn from observations at a relatively small computational cost.
item.dc:creator: James Weber, Makoto Kelp

item.title: Graph-Learned Spring SST Evolution and Land-Ocean Synergy Improve Yangtze Summer Rainfall Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2610.23094v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Seasonal prediction of Yangtze summer rainfall is challenged by nonstationary oceanic precursors. Here we demonstrate that accounting for the evolution of spring SST and state-dependent land surface information improves predictability. Graph total variation (GTV) is applied to March-May SST fields over the western Pacific, Ni\~{n}o3.4, and tropical Indian Ocean to identify spatially coherent, month-specific SST coefficients for each grid cell and month to form a scalar GTV index. The learned coefficient patterns capture April-to-May ENSO decay and an opposing Indian Ocean adjustment, consistent with coupled Indo-Pacific variability. During 2008-2022, the GTV index prediction outperforms Ni\~{n}o3.4-based and sparse-regression benchmarks. Further improvement is achieved by including interactions of May Indo-China Peninsula soil moisture with Indian Ocean SST, importantly also correcting several underestimated wet summers. Circulation diagnostics associate the learned index with a summer geopotential-height dipole and Yangtze moisture convergence, while dry-Indochina/warm-Indian-Ocean conditions coincide with stronger westward extension of the western Pacific subtropical high.
item.dc:creator: Yifu Gao, Haishan Chen, Runze Li, Efi Foufoula-Georgiou, Jasper A. Vrugt

item.title: Energy-Aware Earth System Science: A Community Roadmap
item.description: arXiv:2610.23216v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Earth system models underpin the evidence that informs net-zero policy, yet their energy demands are rarely considered when judging model quality. Using archived output from 159 models spanning five generations of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP), we show that model error has fallen at a constant rate of 13.5 per cent per doubling of compute since 1995. Halving CMIP6 error would require 28 times more compute. Improvements are uneven, with sea-level pressure and surface air temperature errors declining 3.5-fold and 2.7-fold since CMIP1, but precipitation error by only 7 per cent. Machine-learning weather models match or exceed operational forecast skill at a fraction of the runtime, but none publishes measured energy, and including training changes how they rank. We propose a skill-energy framework that combines an empirical Pareto front with a ranking score. These findings argue for standardised reporting of energy use and performance ahead of CMIP8.

item.title: The Atmospheric Chemistry and Surface Interactions on Mars (ACSIOM) Workshop 2025
item.description: arXiv:2610.23500v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The ACSIOM workshop was held in Cambridge from 10th-12th November 2025. Its primary aims were twofold: 1) to gather UK researchers involved in Mars atmospheric science to identify current shortcomings and challenges in the field, and 2) to discuss possible collaborations and future steps needed to maximise the research output from current and future Mars missions. Workshop attendees spanned a wide range of subjects and disciplines, from atmospheric modellers and surface scientists to experimental chemists and Earth/Venus/exoplanet scientists. One of the primary outcomes of the workshop as identified by the attendees was the need for more collaborations between these different communities. It was agreed that we currently lack sufficient interaction between disciplines and this is a key challenge we need to overcome in order to properly utilise and exploit the vast pool of martian expertise available in the UK. Modellers need reaction rates from experimentalists; experimentalists need modelling context to prioritise their experiments; geologists need modelling context to understand the features they see; modellers need geological context to constrain their results. Attendees stressed that the UK Mars community has a critical mass which is internationally recognised, and improving the communication between communities would allow significant progress to be made in martian research, allowing the UK to maintain leadership in Mars science for years to come. We highlight that this is a pivotal moment for such investments as many planetary missions, both for Mars and other terrestrial bodies, are about to be launched or are being considered in the coming years. Having a strong and close-knit community will be key to better identifying needs and capabilities in order to optimise investments in missions and to have the best scientific return possible.
item.dc:creator: Benjamin Benne, Megan A. J. Brown, Bethan S. Gregory, Paul M. Streeter, The ACSIOM Team

item.title: Remote Influences of Land Surface Temperature and their Implications for Sea Surface Temperature Patterns
item.description: arXiv:2603.28481v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The spatial pattern of sea surface temperature (SST) plays a central role in shaping the climate system, yet the influence of land surface temperature (LST) on large-scale SST patterns remains understudied. Using a state-of-the-art coupled climate model, we investigate the climate response to regional abrupt LST warming and time-dependent ramped-warming. We find that regional LST warming can substantially alter the mean-state SST pattern, with the response depending strongly on the location of land warming. In particular, warming over South America strengthens the zonal SST gradient across the tropical Pacific, producing a more La Ni\~na-like mean state. Enhanced land warming increases the zonal contrast in diabatic heating, which excites stationary Rossby wave responses that strengthen alongshore winds and coastal upwelling in the eastern tropical Pacific, providing a dynamical pathway linking regional land warming to changes in the equatorial Pacific mean state. Similar remote SST responses occur for warming over North America, which is accompanied by cooling in the North Pacific, and over Central Africa, which is accompanied by cooling in the tropical Atlantic. In contrast, warming over the Maritime Continent and Tibetan Plateau produces little systematic change in large-scale SST patterns. These results demonstrate that regional LST changes can exert a substantial and geographically dependent influence on remote ocean temperatures. They further suggest that biases in both the mean state and warming trends of LST may contribute to biases in simulated SST patterns in historical simulations, highlighting the importance of accurately representing LST in climate models.
item.dc:creator: Bosong Zhang, Timothy M. Merlis

item.title: Rescene: stable century-long climate emulation from a frozen weather model
item.description: arXiv:2608.09971v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Machine-learning weather models now match or exceed operational numerical prediction in the medium range, but when they are run freely for years they drift, blow up or lose their variability, and dedicated climate emulators are expensive to train. Here we present Rescene, a 0.4 M-parameter wrapper that turns a frozen 1.5$^\circ$, 6-hourly, 69-variable weather model into a stochastic climate emulator. A deterministic slow clock anchors the frozen model to a calendar climatology, and a band-limited AR(1) perturbation, whose spectral envelope is fixed to the observed anomaly spectrum, restores the weather that anchoring removes. A 100-year, 8-member Rescene run shows no detectable drift ($-0.004 \pm 0.014$ K per 100 years), and on the 2022 test year the 16-member ensemble is calibrated (spread/skill 0.89, 0.97 and 0.93 for Z500, T2m and MSLP) with an extratropical synoptic amplitude of 97% of ERA5 on the tuning year. The free run reproduces the geography of day-to-day variability (pattern correlation 0.83 for Z500) and 71% of the observed blocking frequency, where the deterministic wrapper alone has none. Interventions on the frozen operator show a scale-local, approximately linear response in which Z500 perturbations grow upscale 6--14 times more than downscale per 6 h. All constants are fitted on a training year against a rule declared beforehand, and we show that common evaluation shortcuts would have overstated variability and skill. Rescene makes an existing weather model usable for century-long ensembles at negligible training cost.
item.dc:creator: Minjong Cheon

item.title: NeuralDMD: Interpretable Neural Representation of Dynamics from Sparse and Noisy Measurements
item.description: arXiv:2507.03094v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Many challenges in scientific imaging involve solving ill-posed inverse problems, where the goal is to recover spatio-temporal fields from indirect, noisy, and highly sparse measurements - often without access to ground truth data or reliable simulators. To address this challenging scenario, we present NeuralDMD, an interpretable, untrained (per-instance) reconstruction framework that combines neural implicit representations with Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) to reconstruct continuous spatio-temporal dynamics directly from measurements. NeuralDMD parameterizes DMD modes as continuous neural fields, and imposes a low-rank linear dynamics prior with spectral time evolution to enforce temporal continuity. This formulation enables both forecasting under sparsity, and yields interpretable modes and spectra. We find that NeuralDMD outperforms baselines on a wide variety of tasks: from weather data assimilation from sparse station observations to interferometric (Fourier domain) observations of Sagittarius A, the black hole at the center of our galaxy. Moreover, NeuralDMD remains stable when extrapolating into the future. While this framework is most naturally suited to linear dynamics, we show that it can be applied to nonlinear regimes, though with extrapolation performance that degrades with increasing nonlinearity. Together, these results show that NeuralDMD enables interpretable reconstruction and forecasting of spatio-temporal dynamics directly from sparse and indirect measurements without relying on numerical simulators or training data.
